nameStory: Moth mullein gets its name from its delicate flowers that supposedly attract moths, unlike its fuzzy cousin great mullein. The word 'mullein' comes from the old French 'moleine,' which meant soft - though this species is much less soft and fuzzy than other mulleins. Some say the flowers' pale colors and evening blooming habits reminded early botanists of the moths that visited them.
description: Moth mullein is a slender, upright plant that grows 2-4 feet tall with a distinctive spike of small, five-petaled flowers. Unlike its famous fuzzy relative great mullein, this plant has smooth, dark green leaves and a more delicate appearance. It's a biennial, spending its first year as a low rosette of leaves before shooting up a flowering stalk in its second year. The flowers can be white, yellow, or sometimes pink, each about an inch across with prominent purple stamens.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small five-petaled flowers about an inch across, usually white or yellow with bright purple fuzzy stamens that look like tiny bottle brushes - these purple stamens are the key identifying feature

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Smooth, hairless leaves that feel almost waxy to the touch - completely different from the woolly-soft leaves of great mullein; leaves are lance-shaped and have toothed edges

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, slender spike reaching 2-4 feet with flowers scattered along the upper portion rather than packed densely together; much more delicate-looking than the thick, club-like great mullein

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small round capsules about the size of a peppercorn that split open to release tiny seeds; capsules remain on the dried stalk through winter

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Smooth, green to reddish stems that feel firm and slightly ridged when you run your finger along them - no fuzziness whatsoever

habitat: Moth mullein thrives in disturbed soils and sunny, open areas throughout New England's lower elevations. You'll find it along roadsides, in old fields, vacant lots, and construction sites where the soil has been churned up. It prefers well-drained soils and full sun, often appearing in the same weedy areas as chicory, Queen Anne's lace, and evening primrose.

seasonality.spring: First-year plants form low rosettes of smooth, dark green leaves. Second-year plants begin sending up their flowering stalks in late spring.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming time from June through August, with flowers opening sporadically along the spike. Individual flowers last just one day but new ones keep opening over several weeks.
seasonality.fall: Flowering continues into early fall, with seed capsules forming and beginning to dry. Leaves may start yellowing and the plant begins preparing for winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Dried stalks with small round seed capsules persist through winter, looking like thin brown candles dotted with tiny bells. First-year rosettes may stay green under snow.

funFact: Each moth mullein flower opens for just one day - they're like botanical mayflies! The flowers typically open in late afternoon and close by the next morning, which is why you might walk past the same plant and see completely different flowers from one day to the next.
confusionNotes: Most people confuse moth mullein with great mullein, but there's an easy memory trick: moth mullein is 'moth-er smooth' while great mullein is 'greatly fuzzy.' The purple bottle-brush stamens in moth mullein's flowers are also a dead giveaway - great mullein has yellow stamens.
contextualKnowledge: Though considered invasive and even declared a noxious weed in some states like Colorado, moth mullein is generally less aggressive than many introduced plants. It originally came from Europe and North Africa, brought over likely as a garden ornamental or accidentally with other seeds.
compareHints: Among New England's mulleins, moth mullein stands out for its smooth leaves and scattered flower arrangement. Great mullein has thick, woolly leaves and densely packed yellow flowers, while dark mullein has purple stamens like moth mullein but much fuzzier leaves. Orange mullein is rare here but has orange flowers and fuzzy foliage.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Great mullein is much larger and more robust than its relatives like moth mullein, which has a more branched, delicate appearance with less fuzzy leaves.
Orange mullein is distinguished from great mullein by its bright golden-orange flowers rather than pale yellow ones, and its leaves tend to clasp the stem more distinctly.
Among the mullein family in New England, dark mullein is unique for its combination of yellow flowers with dark purple stamens and multiple flowering stems.
Dense-flowered mullein differs from great mullein by having more tightly packed flowers with virtually no branching of the flower spike, while great mullein typically shows some small branches.
Purple mullein's vibrant purple flowers instantly separate it from great mullein's yellow blooms and much woolier leaves.
White mullein stands out from other mullein species by its loosely arranged flowers on individual stalks and its two-toned leaves that are much darker on top than underneath.
Among the mullein family, showy mullein stands out with its large branching flower clusters, while most other mulleins like great mullein have flowers arranged in simple spikes.
